lesson.title: Why You Cannot Just Multiply the Derivatives
lesson.summary: Differentiating a product of two functions is not as simple as multiplying their derivatives; a careful limit argument shows the correct rule and why it must have two terms.
lesson.body:
A natural but wrong guess is that the derivative of a product f(x)g(x) should just be f'(x)g'(x). A quick check kills this idea. Let f(x) = x and g(x) = x, so f(x)g(x) = x^2, whose derivative, by the power rule you already know from the basic derivative rules, is 2x. But f'(x)g'(x) = 1*1 = 1, which is nowhere close to 2x. Something more subtle is going on, and the limit definition of the derivative reveals exactly what.

Start from the definition applied to the product: d/dx [f(x)g(x)] = lim(h to 0) [f(x+h)g(x+h) - f(x)g(x)] / h. The numerator mixes four values together, and the trick that unlocks it is to insert a term that is both added and subtracted, so nothing actually changes: f(x+h)g(x+h) - f(x+h)g(x) + f(x+h)g(x) - f(x)g(x). Grouping the first two terms and the last two terms separately gives f(x+h)[g(x+h) - g(x)] + g(x)[f(x+h) - f(x)]. Dividing by h and splitting into two separate limits, the expression becomes lim f(x+h) * [g(x+h)-g(x)]/h + lim g(x) * [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h.

As h approaches 0, the bracketed pieces are exactly the difference quotients that define g'(x) and f'(x). The factor f(x+h) approaches f(x) because a differentiable function is automatically continuous. Putting the pieces together gives the product rule: d/dx [f(x)g(x)] = f(x)g'(x) + g(x)f'(x). Every term in this sum has one function left alone and the other function differentiated, which explains why the wrong guess f'g' fails: differentiating a product genuinely requires two separate contributions, one from each factor changing while the other is held fixed for a moment.

A fully worked example makes this concrete and checkable. Let h(x) = (x^2 + 1)(x^3 - 2x), with f(x) = x^2 + 1 so f'(x) = 2x, and g(x) = x^3 - 2x so g'(x) = 3x^2 - 2. The product rule gives h'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x) = 2x(x^3 - 2x) + (x^2+1)(3x^2-2). Expanding the first term gives 2x^4 - 4x^2. Expanding the second gives 3x^4 - 2x^2 + 3x^2 - 2 = 3x^4 + x^2 - 2. Adding these together yields 2x^4 - 4x^2 + 3x^4 + x^2 - 2 = 5x^4 - 3x^2 - 2.

This can be checked completely independently by multiplying out h(x) first and differentiating term by term. h(x) = (x^2+1)(x^3-2x) = x^5 - 2x^3 + x^3 - 2x = x^5 - x^3 - 2x. Differentiating directly gives h'(x) = 5x^4 - 3x^2 - 2, which matches the product rule result exactly. Whenever both factors are simple polynomials you can always cross check this way, and doing so a few times is the best way to build confidence that f(x)g'(x) + g(x)f'(x) is really the correct pattern, not just a rule to memorize.

A geometric picture reinforces why two terms are needed instead of one. Imagine f(x) and g(x) as the two side lengths of a rectangle, so the product f(x)g(x) is its area. When x increases by a tiny amount, both sides stretch a little, and the rectangle gains a thin strip along the top with area roughly f(x) times the change in g, plus a thin strip along the side with area roughly g(x) times the change in f. There is also a tiny corner piece where both strips overlap, but that corner shrinks so much faster than the two strips as the change gets small that it disappears in the limit. What survives is exactly f(x)g'(x) + g(x)f'(x), the two strips and nothing else, which is a visual reason the rule has precisely two additive terms rather than one multiplied term.
